passages.t: Short of days and full of trouble
passages.happening:
“Man, who is born of woman, is short of days and full of trouble. Like a flower, he comes forth, then withers away; like a fleeting shadow, he does not endure” (verses 1-2).

“Do You open Your eyes to one like this? Will You bring him into judgment before You? Who can bring out clean from unclean? No one!” (verses 3-4).

A man's days are numbered and his limits set by God. So, Job asks, “look away from him and let him rest, so he can enjoy his day as a hired hand” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
This chapter ends Job's long reply and closes the first round of the debate. Job is still speaking to God, but the tone changes from legal argument to meditation. He steps back from his own case to look at the human condition itself.

Born of woman is a Hebrew way of saying every human being. The opening line has been read at funerals for centuries.

Unclean, tame, is a word from Israel's purity laws for what cannot come into God's presence. Job's question in verse 4 asks whether anything born of human beings can be pure before God. He sees that human frailty includes moral impurity.

The hired hand returns from chapter 7: a laborer who at least has the end of the day and his wages to look forward to. Job asks for that much rest.
passages.asks: Job looked at how short a human life is and asked God for rest. Ask how you are spending days you know are numbered. And ask whom you could give a little rest to this week.

passages.happening:
“For there is hope for a tree: If it is cut down, it will sprout again, and its tender shoots will not fail” (verse 7). Even if its roots grow old and its stump dies in the ground, ‘at the scent of water it will bud and put forth twigs like a sapling’ (verse 9).

“But a man dies and is laid low; he breathes his last, and where is he?” (verse 10). As water disappears from the sea and a river dries up, ‘so a man lies down and does not rise’ (verse 12). Until the heavens are gone, he will not wake.
passages.hearers:
Anyone who farmed in the eastern Mediterranean knew this tree. Olives, sycamores and others can be cut to the stump and still send up new shoots from the root, sometimes years later, once rain comes. Job's point is the reverse of hope: a tree has that hope, and a man does not.

The word hope, tiqvah, frames the chapter. There is hope for a tree here, and in verse 19 God destroys the hope of man.

In most of the Old Testament, the dead go down to Sheol, a shadowy place with no work, no praise of God and no return (Psalm 6:5; Ecclesiastes 9:10). Job's picture of the grave is a dark one, and he speaks from inside it.
passages.later: Isaiah takes up the picture of the stump that sprouts to speak of hope for David's line: “Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit” (Isaiah 11:1).
passages.asks: Job envied a tree its hope. Ask what your own hope rests on when you think about death. And ask whether you have let yourself ask Job's question in verse 10 honestly.

passages.t: When a man dies, will he live again?
passages.happening:
Then, for a moment, a daring wish. “If only You would hide me in Sheol and conceal me until Your anger has passed! If only You would appoint a time for me and then remember me!” (verse 13).

“When a man dies, will he live again? All the days of my hard service I will wait, until my renewal comes. You will call, and I will answer; You will desire the work of Your hands” (verses 14-15). Then God would count his steps but not keep track of his sin. ‘My transgression would be sealed in a bag, and You would cover over my iniquity’ (verse 17).

But the hope fades. As a mountain crumbles and water wears away stone, ‘so You destroy a man’s hope’ (verse 19). God overpowers him and sends him away. If his sons are honored he does not know it, and if they are brought low he is unaware. ‘He feels only the pain of his own body and mourns only for himself’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
In verse 14 Job asks a question the Old Testament rarely asks so openly. He does not assume that the dead will rise. He imagines it as a wish, something God could do if he chose, and then lets the thought go.

Renewal, chaliphah, is the word for a change of clothes or the relief of a soldier on watch. Job pictures himself as a soldier waiting for the one who will take over his post.

The sealed bag in verse 17 draws on the practice of tying up and sealing valuables or records so that no one could open them. Job pictures God tying up his sins and putting them away, not to keep them as evidence but to be done with them.

The chapter ends with erosion: mountains crumbling and stones worn smooth. It is the first of several moments in the book where Job reaches beyond the grave, a line of thought that returns more strongly in chapters 16 and 19.
passages.later: Later Scripture says clearly what Job could only wish: “And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.hard:
Did Job believe in life after death?

Interpreters answer differently, and the chapter itself holds both sides. Verses 10 to 12 and 18 to 22 speak of death as final. Verses 13 to 17 express a longing that God would hide him in Sheol and then call him back, and verse 14 says he would wait until his renewal comes.

Some read this as a real glimmer of faith in life beyond death, which grows into the confident words of 19:25-27. Others read it as a wish Job himself thinks impossible, since the next verses cancel it. A middle view sees Job reaching for a hope the Old Testament has not yet made clear, able to imagine it but not yet able to hold it. All agree that the question is asked honestly, and that the rest of Scripture takes it up.

Job's wish to be hidden in Sheol (verse 13) is a cry for relief from pain he could not bear.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job asked whether a man who dies will live again, and then waited. Ask what you believe about that question, and why. And ask what it would mean to wait, as Job did, for God to call.
